For twenty-year-old Erik Zepeda, walking to Santa Maria High School by himself was a hard-won victory of personal independence.

Erik lives in a residential care facility for adults with disabilities, managing developmental delays that affect his verbal communication and physical reflexes. After years of riding a special education bus, he worked up the courage last year to begin making the morning half-mile walk to campus on his own.

On the morning of October 21, masked federal immigration enforcement agents conducting roving street operations approached Erik from behind, tackled him onto a patch of grass, and placed him in handcuffs.

According to his former teacher and legal advocates, agents loaded him into a federal vehicle and circled the neighborhood while asking questions. Once they realized he was a United States citizen with identification in his wallet, agents released him onto the sidewalk half a mile from campus without medical evaluation.

Erik walked the remaining distance to school bleeding and in severe pain. Administrators immediately called an ambulance upon seeing his condition, transporting him to Marian Regional Medical Center where medical staff confirmed facial lacerations, a black eye, and a wrist fractured in three places that required surgical repair.

The confrontation sparked massive local outrage, prompting hundreds of high school students across Santa Maria and Lompoc to walk out of class in protest of aggressive street sweeps.

How should federal agencies be held accountable when roving enforcement operations injure innocent American citizens?

#SantaMaria #CivilRights #California

When Senator Joe Biden held up a TEC-9 during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on assault weapons.

In August 1993, then-Senator Joe Biden created one of the most famous visual moments in congressional gun control history when he raised a black Intratec TEC-9 semi-automatic pistol above the dais in the Senate Judiciary Committee.

The story behind the iconic hearing:

• The Catalyst: The hearing took place in the immediate aftermath of the July 1993 mass shooting at 101 California Street in San Francisco, where a gunman armed with modified TEC-9 pistols killed eight people.

• The Demonstration: As Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Biden held up the firearm during testimony to argue that weapons with military-style features—such as barrel shrouds, threaded barrels, and high-capacity magazines—served no legitimate sporting or hunting purpose.

• The Legislative Legacy: That hearing provided the critical political momentum for the landmark 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban, passed as part of the 1994 Crime Bill, which banned the TEC-9 by name alongside 18 other models and restricted civilian magazines over 10 rounds for a decade before sunsetting in 2004.

More than three decades later, this image remains one of the defining symbols of the modern Second Amendment debate on Capitol Hill.

Looking back thirty years later, did the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban actually move the needle on violent crime, or did it primarily target cosmetic firearm features?

Be honest — would you vote for Marco Rubio if he ran for president in 2028?

As political strategists, commentators, and primary voters begin looking ahead toward the next national election cycle, Florida Senator Marco Rubio continues to generate intense debate across conservative circles as a potential contender for the Oval Office.

First elected to the U.S. Senate in 2010, Rubio has built a formidable legislative profile in Washington. As the vice chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and a senior member of the Foreign Relations Committee, he has long served as one of the party’s most prominent voices on national security, countering foreign influence, and Latin American diplomacy.

Over the years, Rubio has adapted his policy focus to bridge traditional conservative principles with working-class economic populism, championing domestic manufacturing protections, child tax credit expansions, and aggressive supply-chain decoupling from adversarial foreign nations.

His supporters argue his combination of executive-level foreign policy depth, articulate communication style, and deep electoral strength in Florida make him an experienced candidate capable of uniting different factions of the coalition. Others question whether primary voters will favor an established Washington lawmaker or look toward a fresh governor or populist outsider.

Where do you stand?

Would Marco Rubio have your vote in 2028?

An eighteen-year-old detention officer in Texas threw away her career in uniform for five seconds of viral attention.

Karla Beltran had been on the job for barely three months as a probationary detention deputy with the Bexar County Sheriff’s Office in San Antonio. Instead of maintaining vigilance inside the Bexar County Adult Detention Center, she pulled out a phone while on duty and posed for selfies alongside incarcerated women held behind a glass partition.

The photos captured Beltran flashing peace signs, sticking her tongue out, throwing up hand gestures, and posing while the inmates behind her matched the poses.

Once the images hit social media, Bexar County Sheriff Javier Salazar moved swiftly to fire her on the spot, citing severe breaches of jail security and a total disregard for the standards of the badge.

The dismissal has triggered intense debate across law enforcement and social media circles. Critics question why an eighteen-year-old was placed in charge of guarding adult inmates in the first place, while others point out that anyone prioritizing online clout over facility security belongs nowhere near a correctional environment.

Did the department move too quickly on an eighteen-year-old rookie, or was immediate termination the only acceptable response?

When Donald Trump took to Truth Social to publicly offer the job of White House Press Secretary to UFC CEO Dana White, the internet thought it was classic Trump theater.

Trump urged his longtime friend to take the podium and even suggested bringing along world-champion mixed martial arts fighters as assistants to take on the White House press corps.

Hours later, social media users uncovered a scenario that set the political world on fire.

During Trump’s first administration, the chief spokesperson for the Department of Defense was an experienced communications professional named Dana W. White. A veteran Capitol Hill press secretary and Pentagon official under Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, Dana W. White has spent decades handling hard-hitting questions from national defense reporters.

Now, political observers and commentators are asking whether someone handed Trump a briefing note suggesting "Dana White" for the vacant podium, and instead of calling his former Pentagon spokesperson, Trump reached out to the fight promoter.

Whether this was an intentional publicity blitz or a name confusion on par with Four Seasons Total Landscaping, critics and supporters alike agree on one thing.

Nobody in the room would ever admit it either way.

Did Trump mean to tap his former Pentagon spokesperson, or did he really want UFC chaos in the James S. Brady briefing room?

#DanaWhite #WhiteHouse #Trump

Lance Corporal Thomas Adametz secured a Fallujah house with his platoon. Suddenly, an insurgent force between 50 and 100 strong ambushed their position with grenades, RPGs, and automatic weapons. On the rooftop, numerous Marines were wounded, 4 seriously. One Marine went down, dropping his Squad Automatic Weapon. LCpl Adametz took over the machine gun and went to work. Completely exposed, Adametz laid down suppressive fire, driving back the enemy now just yards away from the Marines' building and allowing the evacuation of the wounded. When the barrel of his SAW warped and overheated, Adametz severely burned his hand, removing it. He ignored the burns, inserted a new barrel, and continued firing. His actions allowed the successful medevacs and played a key role in preventing their position from being overrun. For his heroic initiative and courage, Adametz was awarded the Silver Star.

"...serving as a Rifleman, Echo Company, Second Battalion, First Marines, on 26 April 2004. Following the seizure of two key buildings along a vital avenue of approach into the company's sector, LCpl Adametz and his squad moved into the northernmost building and provided security for his platoon's position. The enemy's fierce attack of RPGs and hand grenades on his platoon's position resulted in four serious and numerous minor casualties. With disregard for his own safety, LCpl Adametz exposed himself to grenades and small arms fire in order to provide suppressive fire, facilitating the evacuation of the wounded Marines. Picking up a SAW from a wounded Marine, he delivered withering fire on enemy forces 25 meters away. LCpl Adametz' aggressive actions and devastating fire were critical in repelling the enemy's attack."

On the left is what internet culture thinks a dangerous operator looks like: full sleeves, a thick beard, tactical gear, and a scowl.

On the right is what actual lethality looks like: a quiet, mild-mannered man with wire-rimmed glasses who looks like an accountant—Sergeant Major Mike Vining (U.S. Army, Ret.).

Don't let the smile fool you. Mike Vining is one of the most lethal, decorated, and revered warriors in the history of American Special Operations.

Look closely at the uniform:

Combat Infantryman Badge (CIB)

Master Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Badge

Master Parachutist Badge with Combat Jump Star

Military Free Fall (HALO) Parachutist Badge

Legion of Merit & Bronze Star Medal

Drafted in 1968, Vining served in Vietnam disarming booby traps, unexploded ordnance, and clearing enemy tunnel complexes under fire.

In 1978, when Colonel Charles Beckwith created 1st SFOD-D (Delta Force) to be America's premier counter-terrorist unit, Mike Vining answered the call. He passed the inaugural selection course and became a founding operator of Delta Force.

Over his career, SGM Vining served on the frontlines of history:

Operation Eagle Claw (1980): Part of the Delta assault force in the Iranian desert.

Operation Urgent Fury (1983): Assaulted the Richmond Hill prison in Grenada, surviving an anti-aircraft shootdown into the sea.

Operation Desert Storm (1991): Hunting Scud missile launchers deep behind enemy lines in Iraq.

The loudest men in the room are rarely the most dangerous.

The truly lethal ones are the quiet professionals who never brag, never posture, and carry decades of silent master craftsmanship in their trade.

Never judge a warrior by his appearance.

In the spring of 2002, Pat Tillman had the world at his feet.

At twenty-five years old, he had defied the odds as a seventh-round draft pick to become a starting safety for the Arizona Cardinals, breaking franchise tackle records and earning the respect of players across the NFL. The team placed a three-year, 3.6 million dollar contract extension on the table.

Then came the morning of September 11, 2001.

Deeply shaken by the attacks on America, Tillman looked around at his life and decided that some things were bigger than football, fame, or financial security. In May 2002, without seeking publicity or fanfare, he turned down the multi-million dollar contract and walked into an Army recruiting station alongside his younger brother Kevin.

The two brothers volunteered for the infantry, completed airborne training, and earned their tan berets in the elite 2nd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment.

Tillman deployed to Iraq during the opening invasion in 2003, returned stateside to graduate from Ranger School, and deployed again to eastern Afghanistan in early 2004. On April 22, 2004, while maneuvering aggressively toward enemy positions during a chaotic ambush in Khost Province, Corporal Tillman was tragically killed in a friendly fire incident.

He never asked for a spotlight, refused all media interviews while in uniform, and simply wanted to serve alongside his fellow soldiers as an equal.

Pat Tillman gave up everything the world tells men to chase so that he could stand on the line for his country.

Rangers Lead the Way.

When active gunfire erupted outside his apartment complex near Fort Liberty, Sergeant Brian Lieberman did not barricade his door or wait for backup. An 82nd Airborne Division combat medic, Lieberman sprinted unarmed straight into the courtyard, located a woman suffering from a sucking chest wound, and immediately constructed an airtight seal out of everyday plastic wrap and tape to prevent her lung from collapsing while keeping her stable until civilian paramedics arrived.

According to the official cohort announcement from the Air Force Medical Service, Lieberman was named a 2026 Angel of the Battlefield for his lifesaving actions.

The combat lifesaver instinct never turns off in civilian life. What is your reaction to this paratrooper's composure under fire?

Brett Morganti

Navy Cross
DURING Global War on Terror
Service: Navy

Citation: The President of the United States of America takes pleasure in presenting the Silver Star to Electronics Technician Second Class (SEAL) Brett Morganti, United States Navy, for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity in action against the enemy while serving as a member of a special operations unit conducting combat operations against enemy forces in enemy territory from 3 to 4 March 2002. Petty Officer Morganti displayed extraordinary heroism, superb tactical performance, and inspiring perseverance as a member of a six-man team that flew back into an enemy stronghold atop a 10,000-foot mountain in order to rescue a captured teammate. As automatic fire erupted from an enemy bunker less than five meters ahead of him, Petty Officer Morganti immediately maneuvered to provide covering fire for a wounded teammate. He courageously left his position of cover to pour fire from his M60 machine gun into the enemy bunker, killing several enemies. In the process, he sustained gunshot and fragmentation wounds in both legs. When his team leader ordered the team to break contact, Petty Officer Morganti led the withdrawal as the team's point man, ignoring the intense pain and blood loss from his wounds to maneuver over one kilometer through icy and precipitous terrain to reach a defendable location. Petty Officer Morganti's tactical expertise and courageous efforts significantly attrited the enemy fighters atop the mountain and contributed to their eventual defeat. By his outstanding display of incredible courage, immeasurable perseverance in the face of heavy enemy fire, and complete devotion to duty, Petty Officer Morganti reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service.

Capt. Brian Erickson, a pilot from the 75th Fighter Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor on July 11, 2008.

Capt. Brian Erickson, 75th FS chief of mission planning, earned the medal while deployed to Bagram Air Base, Afghanistan, for providing ground alert close air support to a German Provincial Reconstruction Team that was under nighttime fire from insurgents in a valley of the Hindu-Kush mountains.

"I'm extremely impressed with the way Captain Erickson handled himself out there," said Colonel Kenneth Todorov, 23rd Wing commander, "He provided close air support in hazardous conditions, with no forward air controller and led a successful mission with valor."

On Oct. 16, 2006, Captain Erickson and his wingman, who were then part of the 75th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, received a short-notice call to provide aerial support to six German soldiers trapped between two mountain ranges. They were receiving enemy fire in the form of rocket-propelled grenades, machine guns, and small-arms fire.

Up until the call, previous flights of non-tactical aircraft had been unable to help the stranded PRT due to their location, limited communication capabilities, and lack of moonlight. Without illumination from the moon or another source, the pilots' night vision goggles provided little assistance.

Once he arrived on scene, Captain Erickson determined there was room for only one aircraft above the mountain tops and just below the clouds. He assigned the safe altitude above the clouds to his wingman, who searched for the insurgents' location with his advanced targeting pod and night vision goggles.

As Captain Erickson flew his A-10 deep into the moonless valley, where the only light on the ground was from insurgent weapons fire, his wingman flew above to relay reports about where the weapon bursts were coming from. Before Capt. Erickson could employ any of his own weapons, he needed to determine the exact location of the PRT to avoid friendly fire.

"I initially had my infrared sensor on to pinpoint the location of the insurgents. The problem with using the infrared was that every time a rocket-propelled grenade went off, the glow impeded my ability to navigate the dark canyon. The whole screen would go white, and I couldn't see outside my cockpit. The only solution was to turn the screens off," said Captain Erickson.

After Captain Erickson turned off his infrared sensor, he continued his low-level runs in search of the PRT. This proved an even more difficult task because the PRT's signaling device, an infrared strobe, was malfunctioning, and the German soldiers, who were untrained in communicating with aircraft, continued to take harassing enemy fire. The chaos of the situation was impaired even more by the PRT's limited proficiency in English. These limitations in combination with the enemy fire caused the PRT to provide confusing information on their exact location.

Realizing that time was running out for the PRT, Captain Erickson released a series of covert illumination flares only visible through night vision devices. Able to "see", he used geographic references from the air and ground to narrow down the PRT's location. During this time, the captain and his wingman were able to identify a location where they believed the enemy fire was coming from.

To be sure of the PRT's location, Captain Erickson conducted a low-altitude show-of-force. He flew between the enemy and friendly positions at 2,000 feet and deployed pyrotechnic self-protection flares, which lit the night sky. His hope was that the enemy would alert to his position and break their attack on the PRT long enough for his wingman to search for clues of the enemy's exact position.

"After we located where we thought the insurgents were, I had my wingman light-up the area with his targeting pod," said Captain Erickson. "During this time the weapons-fire against the Germans was also becoming increasingly accurate, and the need to bring the situation to a close was becoming more-and-more imperative. After we were able to determine that we were, in fact, targeting the insurgents and not the pinned-down German PRT team, it was time to take action."

With Captain Erickson's wingman marking the enemy's position with his TGP's infrared pointer, the PRT confirmed the mark as the enemy fire point of origin. In a single pass, Captain Erickson employed 240 30-millimeter rounds from the aircraft's GAU-8 cannon. This completely halted the enemy's fire and saved the lives of six German soldiers.

Captain Erickson and his wingman remained in the area to monitor both the friendly and enemy positions until the Iraqi National Police and International Security Assistance Force Quick Reaction Force were able to reach and recover the PRT and bring them to safety.

Captain Erickson credited the operation's success to his training. Although he was honored to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor for "doing the job he's trained to do," he pointed out a higher honor.

"The real reward was returning those six coalition soldiers safely to the village they were working at as part of the PRT team," said Captain Erickson.

Margaret Bourke-White was already the most famous photographer in America when she talked her way into the Pacific war. LIFE magazine's star shooter flew on bombing missions, dodged flak, and photographed the war in the Pacific so the folks back home could see it.

She was the first woman accredited as a war correspondent, and she earned it the hard way — in the air over enemy territory with a camera instead of a gun. Her images defined how America remembers the war.

May 3, 2016. Tel Skuf, northern Iraq.

A massive armada of over 100 ISIS fighters, backed by armored bulldozers, truck-mounted heavy machine guns, and suicide truck bombs (VBIEDs), smashed through the frontlines and completely surrounded a small team of American advisors and Kurdish Peshmerga forces.

The team was trapped and on the verge of being overrun.

Special Warfare Operator 1st Class Charles Keating IV—known throughout the SEAL community as "Chuck Heavy"—didn't hesitate. He was part of a small Quick Reaction Force (QRF) that sped directly toward the gunfire.

As soon as they breached the town, Keating climbed onto exposed rooftops into direct, unrelenting machine-gun and sniper fire.

Operating with total disregard for his own safety, Keating engaged the assault force from multiple positions. When his primary rifle jammed, he picked up a machine gun. When that ran dry, he grabbed an assault rifle, continually maneuvering across open ground to draw enemy fire away from his trapped brothers.

His relentless, aggressive counter-attack blunted the ISIS advance long enough for coalition air support to arrive and allowed the surrounded team to break out.

During the final wave of the battle, Keating was mortally wounded by an enemy sniper. He was 31 years old.

Posthumously awarded the Silver Star with Valor and promoted to Chief Petty Officer, Charles Keating IV lived and died by the warrior's creed: put the lives of your brothers above your own.

With a headband, a cigar, and an MK48 machine gun, Chuck Heavy was an absolute force of nature.

Healthcare costs for military families are set to jump sharply again.

The Defense Health Agency (DHA) has confirmed that monthly premiums for TRICARE Young Adult (TYA)—which covers unmarried military dependents ages 21 to 26—will increase by an average of 11% starting in 2027.

The new monthly rates will hit military parents hard:

TRICARE Young Adult Prime: Surging to $893 per month (over $10,700 a year for a single child)

TRICARE Young Adult Select: Rising to $394 per month (over $4,700 a year)

The reason for the massive price tag? By federal statute, the TRICARE Young Adult program receives zero government subsidy. By law, the premiums must cover 100% of the actual estimated healthcare costs delivered to young adult beneficiaries.

This puts military families at a stark disadvantage compared to the civilian world, where the Affordable Care Act allows civilian parents to keep their adult children on employer-sponsored health plans up to age 26 at standard, subsidized dependent rates.

For active-duty service members, retirees, and veterans trying to support college students or young adults just entering the workforce, paying nearly $900 a month per dependent out-of-pocket is becoming unsustainable.

Should Congress pass legislation to subsidize healthcare coverage for military dependents the same way civilian employers do, or is the current system fair?

In 1942, Susan Ahn Cuddy became the first Asian American woman to join the U.S. Navy — while America was at war with Japan. The daughter of a famous Korean independence activist, she served in the WAVES as a code room officer and Link trainer instructor, teaching pilots the skills that kept them alive.

She rose to lieutenant, worked in naval intelligence, and spent her life breaking barriers the way she broke codes: quietly, completely, and first. A pioneer in every sense of the word.

True leadership is not tested when the waters are calm. It is revealed when everything is on the line.

Senior Chief Cryptologic Technician Leslie Allison Bruner gave sixteen years of her life to the United States Navy, deploying to Afghanistan to deliver critical intelligence support alongside Naval Special Warfare units. Known across her commands as an exceptionally brilliant analyst and an unshakeable teammate, she brought energy, fierce loyalty, and laughter into every room she entered.

When she received a cancer diagnosis, she faced the fight with the exact same fearless resolve she brought to the fleet. For three years, through relentless medical treatments, hospital visits, and physical toll, Leslie refused to let the disease dim her spirit or interrupt her dedication to her sailors and her country.

One of the most inspiring moments of her career came when she earned advancement to Senior Chief Petty Officer. Standing tall in her khakis, completely bald from chemotherapy, she beamed with a radiant smile as her fellow sailors pinned the gold anchors onto her collar.

Senior Chief Bruner passed away on August 7, 2017, at thirty-five years old, and was laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.

Her courage, infectious joy, and refusal to surrender define what it means to be a United States Navy Chief.

Fair winds and following seas, Senior Chief. We have the watch.

#USNavy #SeniorChief #ArlingtonNationalCemetery

They called her "Madame X," and the Japanese never knew her name. Agnes Meyer Driscoll joined naval intelligence after World War I and spent the 1920s and 1930s breaking Japan's naval codes — including the "Red Book Code" the Japanese thought was unbreakable.

Her work laid the foundation for everything the Navy's codebreakers achieved at Coral Sea and Midway. She trained a generation of cryptanalysts, and her fingerprints are on every American naval victory of the early Pacific war. The quietest genius of the war.

#AgnesMeyerDriscoll #Codebreaker #MadameX #USNavy #WWIIHistory

When twenty-six-year-old Sergeant Cameron Meddock deployed to Afghanistan for the second time, he was carrying the promise of a growing family back home.

A native of Spearman, Texas, Meddock enlisted in the U.S. Army in 2014, earning his tan beret and joining Company A, 2nd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment at Joint Base Lewis-McChord. Throughout his service, he operated as a machine gunner, automatic rifleman, gun team leader, and fire team leader, embodying the grit and discipline expected of the military’s premier light infantry force.

On January 13, 2019, during combat operations in northwestern Afghanistan’s Badghis Province, Sergeant Meddock was critically wounded by small-arms fire. He was evacuated to Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany, where military support organizations rushed his family to his bedside so they could say their goodbyes before he passed away on January 17.

Back home, his wife Stevie was twenty weeks pregnant with their first child.

Months later, Stevie gave birth to a healthy baby girl named Brinley, a daughter who will grow up learning about the courage, honor, and selfless dedication of a father who gave everything on the front lines before he ever had the chance to hold her.

Rangers Lead the Way.

What the heck are they doing over there in Michigan?

In a move that has people across the country doing a double take, the city council of Hamtramck, Michigan, officially voted to amend its local animal ordinance to allow residents to perform animal sacrifices on residential property for religious ceremonies.

The policy change follows months of intense community debate over traditional observances like Eid al-Adha, where livestock such as goats and sheep are prepared for holiday meals and shared with neighbors and families in need. City officials and municipal legal advisers insisted that banning the practice outright would violate First Amendment rights and run afoul of longstanding United States Supreme Court rulings protecting religious rituals from government interference.

Under the updated rules, residents who plan to conduct an animal sacrifice at home are required to notify city hall in advance, pay a permit fee, and adhere to strict sanitation and disposal standards to keep the practice out of public view. While proponents celebrated the decision as an essential victory for constitutional freedom, neighbors and community members have pushed back hard, raising serious concerns regarding residential zoning, sanitation enforcement, and suburban neighborhood standards.

Where should the line be drawn between protecting constitutional religious freedom and enforcing neighborhood residential rules?

#Michigan #Hamtramck #FirstAmendment

Robert Leckie landed on Guadalcanal with the 1st Marine Division in 1942 and fought through one of the most brutal campaigns of the war — malaria, hunger, and Japanese attacks in the jungle dark. He came home and wrote "Helmet for My Pillow," the memoir that gave the Pacific war its voice.

Decades later, his story reached millions through the miniseries "The Pacific." Leckie never claimed to be a hero. He just told the truth about what ordinary Marines did in extraordinary places.

#RobertLeckie #Guadalcanal #HelmetForMyPillow #USMarines #WWIIHistory

“A DAYLIGHT ATTACK. AN INCOMING GRENADE. A SPLIT SECOND TO SAVE NICK.” — How Marine Kyle Carpenter Survived the Unsurvivable.

On November 21, 2010, inside the violent insurgent stronghold of Marjah, Helmand Province, Afghanistan, 21-year-old Marine Lance Corporal William "Kyle" Carpenter was manning a sandbagged rooftop security post at Observation Post Dakota alongside his close friend, Lance Corporal Nicholas Eufrazio.

During a coordinated daylight Taliban assault, enemy fighters lobbed hand grenades over the compound wall:

One grenade bounced onto the small rooftop, landing directly between Carpenter and Eufrazio. There was nowhere to run and no time to kick it away.

Without hesitation, Carpenter lunged forward and threw his entire body on top of the live grenade—using his plate carrier and helmet to absorb the full, concentrated force of the detonation.

The blast shrapnel shattered Carpenter’s skull, collapsed his right lung, blew out his right eye, broke his jaw in dozens of places, and severely mangled his right arm. First responders initially found him without a pulse.

After flatlining on the operating table, undergoing more than 40 surgeries, and spending nearly three years at Walter Reed, Kyle Carpenter miraculously survived. His sacrifice also saved Nick Eufrazio’s life.

On June 19, 2014, Carpenter was awarded the Medal of Honor, becoming the youngest living recipient of America’s highest military decoration for valor.

The Next Generation Squad Weapon program isn't just replacing the M4—it's also replacing the battle-tested FN M249 SAW with the Sig Sauer XM250.

Eugene Sledge was a 19-year-old Marine mortarman when he landed on Peleliu — a coral rock the Marines called the bitterest battle of the war. Then came Okinawa: 82 days of rain, mud, and close combat that broke men around him.

He came home, became a biology professor, and finally wrote what he had seen: "With the Old Breed." It is the truest American memoir of the Pacific war — no glory, no varnish, just what one young man endured and what it cost him. The photo here shows him on Okinawa in 1945, weeks after the fighting ended.

#EugeneSledge #WithTheOldBreed #Peleliu #Okinawa #WWIIHistory

ZERO ROOM FOR ERROR.” — An authentic look at one of the most iconic photographs in special operations history, capturing Major Thomas Greer (aka “Dalton Fury”) and Sergeant Major John “Shrek” McPhee (aka “The Sheriff of Baghdad”) staging outside an armored vehicle during the height of combat operations in Iraq.

Roy Geiger was a Marine aviator who kept rising until there was nowhere left to rise. He led Marine air wings at Guadalcanal, then commanded the III Amphibious Corps at Bougainville and Guam.

At Okinawa, when Army General Simon Buckner was k*lled in action, Geiger took command of the entire Tenth Army — the only Marine in history to command a field army. He finished the battle, then quietly handed it back. A Marine's Marine, to the very end.

#RoyGeiger #Okinawa #USMarines #TenthArmy #WWIIHistory

On November 3, 2026, Spokane County SWAT deputies were dispatched to a rural property near Spangle, Washington, after an injured woman reached a neighbor’s home seeking emergency aid. Law enforcement quickly confirmed an active domestic crisis where an armed suspect had taken the lives of his mother and sister before barricading himself inside the residence.

Knowing that innocent lives hung in the balance, SWAT team members moved in to rescue potential survivors and secure the home. As Deputy Parker Perry, a dedicated K9 handler with his partner Brego, and Deputy Mason Acheson, an experienced SWAT sniper and former Washington State Trooper, advanced toward the entrance, the barricaded suspect opened fire without warning.

Both deputies were critically injured in the ambush while shielding their fellow officers. Team members immediately returned fire, safely pulled their wounded brothers from the line of fire, and contained the scene. Deputy Acheson, 35, passed away the following morning. Deputy Perry, 29, remained on life support until his family made the selfless choice to donate his organs, continuing to save lives even after his final watch.

Both men were Washington Army National Guard veterans, devoted husbands, and loving fathers who left behind young children, with Deputy Perry’s wife currently expecting their third baby. Their courage, quiet dedication, and willingness to place themselves in harm’s way to protect their community will endure forever.

How will you honor the legacy of these two brave deputies who gave everything to protect their community?

#FallenHeroes #SpokaneCounty #LawEnforcement

They called him "Howlin' Mad" — and he earned it. Holland Smith spent the years between the wars figuring out how to land an army on a defended beach, writing the doctrine the entire Pacific war would run on.

At Tarawa, Saipan, Tinian, and Iwo Jima, it was Smith's amphibious machine that put Marines ashore and kept them supplied. Blunt, demanding, and usually right, he forged the modern Marine Corps in the fire of the island-hopping campaign.

#HollandSmith #AmphibiousWarfare #USMarines #IwoJima #WWIIHistory

Gunnery Sgt. Aubrey McDade
1st Battalion, 8th Marines
Fallujah, Iraq, Nov. 11, 2004
Award: Navy Cross

If you asked Maj. Michael DuCharme why he joined the Army, he will tell you that God called him. There were few people in his family who had served; he was nearing the age requirement where he would have been too old. And, in 2002, we were already in the war, so his wife and he knew it would mean deployment, according to DuCharme.

He deployed to Baghdad first in 2004 and then again in 2006 as a Regular Army officer. He continues to serve as an active Army Reservist.

As a chaplain in Iraq, he provided religious support and counseling services for a battalion of over 1,200 soldiers, mostly military police. These soldiers were spread out all over the city of Baghdad, with some of the units stationed much further away in the region. DuCharme had to travel to visit the soldiers in the places where they resided, which meant taking the same roads the soldiers took when they went out on patrols and missions.

“It was a three-hour road trip to get to some of the guys,” he said. “My truck was as likely to get hit as anybody else's.”

DuCharme explained that there was a benefit to being out in the field and on the road like any other soldier. “If I went around on a regular basis...there was only one reason that I was doing it, and that was to see them [the troops],” he said.

And traveling affected the way DuCharme was able to communicate with soldiers about God.

“When I was talking, counseling with soldiers about faith in God...I had to take my own medicine,” he said. “Prior to that I had faith; but it wasn't the kind of faith where you really had to depend on God.”

DuCharme performed religious functions by holding chapel services or providing other religious leaders for non-Christian soldiers. But that was only a small part of his job.

“Ninety percent of what I did over there was counseling,” he explained. “I started by building a relationship with the soldiers. Once I saw them four or five times, then they would naturally come to me when they had something to talk about.”

“A chaplain is the only person in the U.S. Army that a soldier has complete confidentiality with. They are able to talk about anything that it on their minds,” he said.

“All of my counseling training is pastoral counseling. I don't have any formal psychological training,” DuCharme said. Therefore, he would ask regular questions and listen to what the soldiers were saying.

“The way I worked was, I would keep asking questions, until God seemed to take the conversation down a road,” he said. “A lot of times it would be directly spiritual. Other times it wouldn't be. I was a friend to them. They could trust me,” he said.

During deployments, “Soldiers were impacted because they were watching friends die. There is a “constant low angst that a soldier has to go through at all times, DuCharme reflected.

“I would talk to them about friends and family, living and dying; all the things that life is about,” he said. “Something I will always have from those deployments is that I could see everyday why God had called me to this.”

DuCharme shared a story of one experience from his first deployment that changed his life. In 2004, he had planned a trip to visit soldiers in a city that was on the opposite side of Baghdad from where he was stationed. When he and the team he was traveling with arrived, the soldiers they had come to see weren't even there -- to his frustration and disappointment. But, because there was a swimming pool at the base and it was a hot day, they decided to stay for a while so some of the team members could go for a swim. DuCharme was sitting at a poolside table when a young female soldier came over, sat down and started talking to him, he said. They ended up talking for over an hour.

“She had been distanced from God,” DuCharme said. But following that conversation, they talked frequently and she started going to chapel services too, he noted. “She ended up getting killed shortly thereafter.” While out in a convoy she was hit under her armor, just a few weeks before she was supposed to go home.

“But I got to talk to her parent's back home,” he said. “It was a relief [for them] knowing that she was walking with God before she died.”

So, what seemed at first like a wasted day at the pool, ended up being a significant part of this young woman's spiritual journey prior to the end of her earthly life. “It was instrumental not only in her life, but also for me in that I was able to share that with her parents,” DuCharme said.

“This is one of many stories, like that,” he said. “God tends to put you in the right place at the right time.”

“[Soldiers] ... face all the things: death, loss, heat, separation from family. And even though it's hard, they go out and do it, day in and day out...with the goal of bringing each other home,” DuCharme said. “When bad things happen, when people die, there is survivor's guilt. Soldiers ask ‘Why not me?' But if you struggle through it with God and others, you ironically come out with a deeper faith,” he said.

“Even with all the bad stuff that happened, I would do it all over again,” DuCharme said.

“Memorial and Veterans Days will never be the same,” DuCharme said. “Those used to be days where I would think about taking a day off. Now I think I celebrate [those holidays] in the way they were meant to be celebrated.”

Chaplain Michael DuCharme received two Bronze Stars, one for each of his deployments.

The 23rd and 24th of June 2006 would be a crucible of leadership and heroism for an already battle-tested and decorated captain in the U.S. Army’s Special Forces. Captain Sheffield F. Ford III was in charge of some 16 Americans and 46 Afghan Army soldiers during "Operation Kaika" in the Panjawi District of Afghanistan’s Kandahar province.

In the bleak farmland, criss-crossed by ditches and barren expanses, Ford led his unit to "re-establish order" in the contested region, entering a Spartan Afghan village on the 23rd. The dilapidated buildings and mud huts were hiding a Taliban force of unknown strength with one thought on their minds: killing Americans and the Afghan soldiers working to take back their country. In their hastily prepared patrol base, Ford organized a perimeter as night enveloped the isolated Special Forces team and their Afghan allies.

As darkness fell, "all hell [broke] loose." From three directions, rifle, machine gun, and rocket-propelled grenade fire landed and exploded on their position. One of Ford’s squad mates later said they had "not seen this disciplined execution of infantry tactics" by the Taliban. Ford dug his men in to repel the assault.

Moving from position to position, he alternated between barking orders, firing at the enemy, and rallying the Afghan soldiers with him. As the night crept on, the remaining Taliban fighters withdrew and Ford took stock of the situation.

Early the next day, he ordered some of his Special Forces operators to lead a team of Afghans into the suspected Taliban hideout. As the unit engaged the hostiles, it was divided in two when some 200 Taliban fighters poured out, separating the American attackers and surrounding the make-shift patrol base.

Over the radio, Ford was connected with one of the translators who had been leading the mission on the Taliban position. The translator saw two Americans were fighting despite being severely wounded and feared capture at any minute. Knowing the ramifications of being taken alive by the Taliban, the translator told Ford he would, if ordered, end the suffering of the troops and his own life rather than be captured. Ford responded, "We’ve got people coming." Ford organized and launched an effective rescue to recover the translator and wounded troops, even if they were mortally wounded. He would not allow American or Afghan alike to be taken in any condition by the Taliban.

The adversaries fought so close to one another that the terrorists screamed to the Afghan soldiers that, "we can forgive you; just put your weapons down and walk away. We want the Americans alive." The months of training and the ties formed between the Americans and the Afghans were put to the test. Seeing the example of Ford running to each of the beleaguered fighters in the face of constant fire, and remembering all they had endured alongside their American trainers, the Afghan soldiers responded to the Taliban’s offer with well-aimed shots and an unbreakable defense.

Exemplifying the U.S. Special Forces motto, De Opresso Liber (to liberate the oppressed), Ford inspired his Afghan troops to stand up to the Taliban fighters and bring them down. He led an evacuation of all the men under his command, wounded included, out of the village under the cover of Apache attack choppers to ensure all would be safe, while sealing the fate of the insurgents. Ford successfully extricated his men, and the unit had more than 120 confirmed kills. Just as the Americans and Afghans had trained together, they sacrificed together; two American and three Afghan soldiers would not leave the battlefield alive. For his accomplishments in the face of such an overpowering force, Ford was awarded the Silver Star, the nation’s third highest military award.

SHOULD FIREARM SAFETY BE TAUGHT IN EVERY PUBLIC CLASSROOM? Tennessee has become the first state in the nation to mandate annual firearm safety classes for all public and charter school students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The landmark law aims to eliminate accidental childhood shootings by removing the dangerous curiosity around guns and teaching kids exactly what to do if they find an unsecured weapon.

“It will save kids, to be honest with you. It avoids some really bad situations. If we teach children from an early age never to touch a firearm and immediately alert an adult, we take away the curiosity that leads to tragedy.”

 Officer Chad Gann, Wildlife Officer & Firearm Instructor, Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security

How the New Law Works
Statewide Annual Mandate: Under Tennessee Code Ann. § 49-6-1016, all public school districts and charter academies across Tennessee must deliver yearly age-appropriate firearm safety lessons developed in partnership with the Department of Education and the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA).

Elementary Curriculum (Grades K–5): Younger children focus strictly on accident avoidance and identifying real firearms versus toys. Lessons reinforce the foundational four-step rule: Stop, don't touch, leave the area, and immediately tell a trusted adult.

Middle & High School Curriculum (Grades 6–12): Older students study safe storage practices, the mechanical risks of handling firearms, hunter safety fundamentals, suicide prevention awareness, and the legal consequences of unlawful possession.

The state statute strictly prohibits live ammunition or working firearms during instruction. Certified School Resource Officers (SROs) and instructors use inert plastic training props, multimedia presentations, and classroom demonstrations.

Supporters emphasize that with over 400 million firearms in circulation across the United States, basic firearm safety is a vital life skill comparable to teaching kids how to swim, look both ways before crossing the street, or practice fire drills. Demystifying guns reduces accidental discharges caused by childish curiosity.

Critics and gun reform advocates contend that the burden of gun safety belongs exclusively on adult gun owners through strict safe-storage laws, arguing that mandatory school instruction risks normalizing weapons in learning environments.
